report.title: Iran-based Cyber Actors Enabling Ransomware Attacks on US Organizations
report.summary: Iran-based cyber actors (Pioneer Kitten/Fox Kitten/UNC757 etc.) have been conducting intrusions since 2017, exploiting public-facing VPNs and web appliances to gain initial access, establishing persistence via web shells and scheduled tasks, collaborating with ransomware affiliates (NoEscape, Ransomhouse, ALPHV) for encryption, and conducting separate espionage operations for the GOI. They use Shodan for reconnaissance, disable security tools, and exfiltrate sensitive data.

behaviors.description: Actors scan Shodan to identify IP addresses hosting devices vulnerable to specific CVEs before exploitation.
behaviors.evidence: The actors have been observed using the Shodan search engine to identify and enumerate IP addresses that host devices vulnerable to a particular CVE.

behaviors.description: Actors exploit public-facing networking devices (Citrix Netscaler, F5 BIG-IP, Pulse Secure/Ivanti VPN, PanOS firewalls, Check Point Gateways) to gain initial access.
behaviors.evidence: Iranian cyber actors scan and exploit public-facing networking devices, including the following devices and associated CVEs: * Citrix Netscaler (CVEs-2019-19781 and CVE-2023-3519) * F5 BIG-IP (CVE-2022-1388) * Pulse Secure/Ivanti VPNs (CVE-2024-21887) * PanOS firewalls (CVE-2024-3400) * Check Point Security Gateways (CVE-2024-24919)

behaviors.description: Actors deploy web shells (version.dll, ctxHeaderLogon.php, etc.) on compromised Netscaler devices for persistent remote access.

observables.note: Web shell observed on compromised devices
Web shell observed on compromised devices

behaviors.evidence: Iranian cyber actors capture login credentials on compromised Netscaler devices via deployed webshell; create a directory on Netscaler devices for webshell deployment; deploy webshells on compromised Netscaler devices in two directories (observed closely after system owning patching); and place the malicious backdoor version.dll.

behaviors.description: Actors create local accounts on victim networks for persistence and lateral movement.

observables.note: Placeholder for newly created account path

behaviors.evidence: Iranian cyber actors create local accounts on victim networks.

behaviors.description: Actors use administrator credentials to disable antivirus and security software on compromised networks.

observables.note: PowerShell commands to disable security tools
Used to run security disable commands

behaviors.evidence: Iranian cyber actors use administrator credentials to disable antivirus and security software.

behaviors.description: Actors lower PowerShell execution policies to a less secure level to enable script execution.
behaviors.evidence: Iranian cyber actors lower PowerShell policies to a less secure level.

behaviors.description: Actors deploy AnyDesk and Meshcentral remote access programs for command and control.
behaviors.evidence: Iranian cyber actors install “AnyDesk” remote access program. Iranian cyber actors deploy Meshcentral to connect with compromised servers for remote access.

behaviors.description: Actors use ligolo/ligolo-ng and ngrok.io for protocol tunneling to create outbound C2 connections.
behaviors.evidence: Iranian cyber actors use ligolo / ligolo-ng for open source tunneling and ngrok[.]io NGROK to create outbound connections to a random subdomain.

behaviors.description: Actors export registry hives and network firewall configurations during discovery phase.
behaviors.evidence: Iranian cyber actors export registry hives and network firewall configurations.

behaviors.description: Actors exfiltrate account usernames from domain controllers and access configuration files and logs.
behaviors.evidence: Iranian cyber actors exfiltrate account usernames from the domain controller and access configuration files and logs.

behaviors.description: Actors collaborate with ransomware affiliates (NoEscape, Ransomhouse, ALPHV) providing network access and strategizing extortion.
behaviors.evidence: After infiltrating victim networks, the actors collaborate with ransomware affiliates (including NoEscape, Ransomhouse, and ALPHV) in exchange for a percentage of the ransom payments by providing affiliates with access to victim networks, locking victim networks, and strategizing to extort victims.

behaviors.description: Actors conduct separate espionage operations stealing sensitive technical data for the GOI from Israel and Azerbaijan networks.

observables.value: Remote Desktop session initiation via admin account
observables.note: Used for initial access and lateral movement

behaviors.evidence: The FBI further assesses these Iran-based cyber actors are associated with the Government of Iran and—separate from the ransomware activity—conduct computer network exploitation activity in support of the GOI (such as intrusions enabling the theft of sensitive technical data against organizations in Israel and Azerbaijan).

behaviors.description: Actors deploy scheduled tasks using DLL side-loading and backdoor techniques for persistence.
behaviors.evidence: Iranian cyber actors implement a scheduled task that uses a DLL side-loading technique and a scheduled task that loads malware through back doors.

behaviors.description: Actors create a directory on Netscaler devices for webshell deployment as part of persistence mechanism.
behaviors.evidence: Iranian cyber actors create a directory on Netscaler devices for webshell deployment; observed closely after system owning patching.

behaviors.description: Actors use valid compromised credentials to log into domain controllers and other infrastructure.

observables.value: Domain admin login via RDP or PowerShell

behaviors.evidence: Iranian cyber actors repurpose administrative credentials of network admins to log into domain controllers and other infrastructure.

candidates.title: Schtasks Scheduled Task Creation With DLL Side-Loading
candidates.rationale: Actors create scheduled tasks via schtasks.exe with '/create /sc onlogon' arguments to achieve persistence through DLL side-loading. The schtasks binary is not a standard Windows utility; its presence combined with these specific arguments is highly distinctive.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate administrative use of schtasks.exe if the tool is used in the environment for task scheduling. Mitigate by verifying the binary is not a known management tool and the command line includes the onlogon trigger with DLL side-loading context.

candidates.title: PowerShell Execution Policy Downgrade To Bypass
candidates.rationale: Actors lower the PowerShell execution policy to 'Bypass' scope 'Process' to enable unrestricted script execution. This specific policy downgrade is a strong indicator of defense evasion and is directly observable in PowerShell script block logging.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Developers or administrators temporarily setting ExecutionPolicy to Bypass for interactive debugging. The rule should require both 'Bypass' and 'Scope Process' to appear together, which is less common in benign interactive use.

candidates.title: Registry Hive Export Of SYSTEM And User Hives
candidates.rationale: Actors export registry hives including the SYSTEM hive and HKCU\Software for offline credential and configuration harvesting. Writing to these high-value hive paths via registry_set events is rare outside of backup/recovery tools.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate backup software (e.g., Windows Backup, Veeam) or system restore operations may export registry hives. Exclude known backup agent image paths; a single event targeting the SYSTEM hive is already suspicious in non-backup contexts.

candidates.title: Netscaler Web Shell File Creation
candidates.rationale: Actors deploy specific web shell files (version.dll, ctxHeaderLogon.php, netscaler.php) on compromised Citrix Netscaler appliances. These filenames are not part of legitimate Netscaler installations and directly indicate persistence backdoors.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Netscaler firmware updates or custom theme deployments might write PHP files to the web directory. The specific names 'version.dll', 'ctxHeaderLogon.php', and 'netscaler.php' are not known legitimate components. Verify against Citrix file manifests.

candidates.title: Ligolo-ng Tunneling Connection To Ngrok
candidates.rationale: Actors use the ligolo-ng tunneling tool to create outbound C2 connections via ngrok.io subdomains. The combination of the ligolo-ng binary (uncommon in enterprise) connecting to ngrok.io is a strong indicator of protocol tunneling for command and control.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Developers or red teams using ligolo-ng and ngrok.io for legitimate tunneling. In most enterprise environments, both the binary and the domain are anomalous. Consider allow-listing known developer workstations.

skipped: B1: Shodan reconnaissance is conducted from attacker infrastructure; DNS queries to shodan.io from internal hosts are not a durable on-host behavior.
B2: Exploitation of public-facing appliances (Citrix, F5, etc.) occurs on the appliance OS, not observable via Windows endpoint telemetry.
B4: Local account creation via 'net user /add' is a valid technique but lower priority than the schtasks persistence mechanism (B13) which is more distinctive.
B5: Antivirus disable via PowerShell cmdlets; covered conceptually by B6 (policy downgrade) and the specific cmdlets are less durable than the policy change.
B7: AnyDesk/Meshcentral are legitimate remote administration tools; high false positive rate in managed environments.
B10: Domain enumeration via dsquery is specific but shares process_creation logsource with higher-priority B13; can be added later.
B11: Ransomware affiliate coordination lacks durable on-host observables.
B12: Espionage RDP usage is generic; no distinctive command-line or binary.
B14: Netscaler webshell deployment directory creation; overlaps with B3 file creation and uses Linux paths not matching Windows file_event.
B15: Valid credential use for DC access is generic RDP; no distinctive on-host behavior.
plan.notes: Selected five candidates across five logsource categories (process_creation, ps_script, registry_set, file_event, network_connection) and four tactics (Persistence, Defense Evasion, Discovery, Command and Control). Prioritized behaviors with distinctive binaries, command lines, or target objects over generic techniques. Skipped IOC-only, appliance-only, or high-FP behaviors.

rules.title: Schtasks Scheduled Task Creation With Onlogon Trigger For Persistence
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Schtasks Scheduled Task Creation With Onlogon Trigger For Persistence
id: a52cc835-e1f1-4341-9a36-263eec53a0f3
status: experimental
description: 'Detects creation of scheduled tasks via schtasks.exe with ''/create /sc onlogon'' arguments indicative of persistence
  mechanisms used by threat actors.'
references:
- 'https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-241a'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.execution
- attack.persistence
- attack.t1053.005
- attack.t1053
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection:
    'Image|endswith': '\schtasks.exe'
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - /create
    - /sc
    - onlogon
  filter_legitimate_admin:
    'ParentImage|endswith':
    - '\mmc.exe'
    - '\taskschd.msc'
  filter_office_integrator:
    ParentImage:
    - 'C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\integration\integrator.exe'
    - 'C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Office\root\integration\integrator.exe'
    'Image|endswith':
    - '\schtasks.exe'
    'CommandLine|contains': 'Microsoft\Office\Office Performance Monitor'
  filter_windows_update:
    'ParentImage|endswith': '\wuauclt.exe'
    'CommandLine|contains': 'Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate\'
  filter_sccm_intune:
    'ParentImage|endswith':
    - '\policyplatform.exe'
    - '\sscmsvc.exe'
    - '\intuneextensionservice.exe'
    'CommandLine|contains': '/create /tn *'
  condition: 'selection and not 1 of filter_*'
falsepositives:
- Legitimate administrative use of schtasks.exe for creating scheduled tasks with onlogon trigger
- Software installation or update processes using schtasks.exe
- Enterprise management tools (SCCM, Intune) creating scheduled tasks during provisioning
level: high

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Schtasks creating scheduled task with onlogon trigger for persistence - typical attacker behavior

tests.label: positive

tests.label: positive

tests.label: negative

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Schtasks with reordered parameters, mixed casing, extra whitespace, and double-quoted task path

tests.label: positive

tests.label: positive

tests.label: positive

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate admin creating scheduled task with onlogon via schtasks but from mmc.exe (filtered by filter_legitimate_admin)

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Office integrator creating performance monitor task (matches filter_office_integrator)

tests.label: negative

tests.label: negative

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE (Image LIKE '%\\schtasks.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%/create%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%/sc%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%onlogon%' ESCAPE '\')) AND (NOT COALESCE(((ParentImage LIKE '%\\mmc.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE '%\\taskschd.msc' ESCAPE '\') OR ((ParentImage LIKE 'C:\\Program Files\\Microsoft Office\\root\\integration\\integrator.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE 'C:\\Program Files (x86)\\Microsoft Office\\root\\integration\\integrator.exe' ESCAPE '\') AND Image LIKE '%\\schtasks.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%Microsoft\\Office\\Office Performance Monitor%' ESCAPE '\') OR (ParentImage LIKE '%\\wuauclt.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%Microsoft\\Windows\\WindowsUpdate\\%' ESCAPE '\') OR ((ParentImage LIKE '%\\policyplatform.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE '%\\sscmsvc.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE '%\\intuneextensionservice.exe' ESCAPE '\') AND CommandLine LIKE '%/create /tn %' ESCAPE '\')), 0))

| where (FolderPath endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and (ProcessCommandLine contains "/create" and ProcessCommandLine contains "/sc" and ProcessCommandLine contains "onlogon")) and (not(((InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\mmc.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\taskschd.msc") or ((InitiatingProcessFolderPath in~ ("C:\\Program Files\\Microsoft Office\\root\\integration\\integrator.exe", "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\Microsoft Office\\root\\integration\\integrator.exe")) and FolderPath endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine contains "Microsoft\\Office\\Office Performance Monitor") or (InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\wuauclt.exe" and ProcessCommandLine contains "Microsoft\\Windows\\WindowsUpdate\\") or ((InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\policyplatform.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\sscmsvc.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\intuneextensionservice.exe") and ProcessCommandLine contains "/create /tn "))))
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE (Image LIKE '%\\schtasks.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%/create%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%/sc%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%onlogon%' ESCAPE '\')) AND (NOT COALESCE(((ParentImage LIKE '%\\mmc.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE '%\\taskschd.msc' ESCAPE '\') OR ((ParentImage LIKE 'C:\\Program Files\\Microsoft Office\\root\\integration\\integrator.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE 'C:\\Program Files (x86)\\Microsoft Office\\root\\integration\\integrator.exe' ESCAPE '\') AND Image LIKE '%\\schtasks.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%Microsoft\\Office\\Office Performance Monitor%' ESCAPE '\') OR (ParentImage LIKE '%\\wuauclt.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%Microsoft\\Windows\\WindowsUpdate\\%' ESCAPE '\') OR ((ParentImage LIKE '%\\policyplatform.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE '%\\sscmsvc.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR ParentImage LIKE '%\\intuneextensionservice.exe' ESCAPE '\') AND CommandLine LIKE '%/create /tn %' ESCAPE '\')), 0))

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 7/7, negatives blocked 7/7, benign hits 0/1200

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P7 demonstrate realistic operator evasions: parameter reordering, extra whitespace, mixed casing, single vs double quotes, UNC target paths, environment variables in arguments, SysWOW64 vs System32 paths, and varied parent processes (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe). All preserve the three required substrings (/create, /sc, onlogon) in CommandLine and keep Image ending with schtasks.exe, so a well-written rule catches them. Negative variants N1-N4 are benign look-alikes that match the selection but are explicitly filtered by the rule's four filter_* clauses (mmc.exe parent, Office integrator path, wuauclt.exe parent, SCCM/Intune parents with /create /tn pattern). Each negative differs in ParentImage and/or CommandLine content from the positives. Out-of-scope variants OOS1-OOS3 represent evasions the current logsource/rule cannot reliably detect: OOS1 renames the binary (rule keys on Image suffix, no OriginalFileName field); OOS2 bypasses schtasks entirely using Task Scheduler COM APIs (no schtasks.exe process); OOS3 hides 'onlogon' behind an environment variable (sensor records literal %TRIGGER_TYPE%, not expanded value). These are reported for analyst awareness; the rule is not expected to match them without additional telemetry.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Renamed schtasks.exe (evil.exe) with OriginalFileName still schtasks.exe - rule keys on Image ending with schtasks.exe so renamed binary evades detection

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses Task Scheduler COM API directly via PowerShell (RegisterTaskDefinition) - no schtasks.exe process creation at all

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses schtasks.exe but with /sc onlogon split across environment variable expansion (sensor records literal %VAR%) - rule needs literal 'onlogon' in CommandLine

rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Export of SYSTEM and User Registry Hives
id: 3b9e0242-1c17-463f-972b-7385b5c2bc12
status: experimental
description: 'Detects attempts to export critical registry hives (SYSTEM and HKCU\Software) which is indicative of credential
  and configuration harvesting by threat actors.'
references:
- 'https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-241a'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.discovery
- attack.t1012
logsource:
  category: registry_set
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_target:
    'TargetObject|endswith':
    - '\SYSTEM'
    - '\Software'
  condition: selection_target
falsepositives:
- Legitimate backup or recovery operations exporting registry hives using known tools like Windows Backup, Veeam, or system
  restore utilities.
level: medium

tests.label: positive

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE TargetObject LIKE '%\\SYSTEM' ESCAPE '\' OR TargetObject LIKE '%\\Software' ESCAPE '\'

conversions.kusto:
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where RegistryKey endswith "\\SYSTEM" or RegistryKey endswith "\\Software"
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE TargetObject LIKE '%\\SYSTEM' ESCAPE '\' OR TargetObject LIKE '%\\Software' ESCAPE '\'

history.summary: 7 evasion variants -> positives 7/7, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/160

rules.redteam_analysis: The rule keys solely on TargetObject ending with '\SYSTEM' or '\Software'. All positive variants preserve those suffixes while varying casing, registry root, user SID, Image path, and Details strings – changes a well-written rule on the registry_set logsource can still catch because the suffix match is case-insensitive and path-agnostic. Negative variants are benign operations that touch registry hives but target different keys (SAM, subkeys of SOFTWARE, SYSTEM\Backup), so they correctly fail the suffix check. Out-of-scope evasions (direct disk reads, kernel memory access) produce no registry_set telemetry at all; the rule cannot see them, and they are reported for analyst awareness rather than as test cases.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker reads hive files directly from disk via Volume Shadow Copy – no registry_set event is generated

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses a kernel driver to parse registry hives from memory – bypasses registry API entirely

history.summary: 7 evasion variants -> positives 7/7, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/160

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants (P4-P7) demonstrate that the rule's endswith logic on TargetFilename correctly catches the malicious filenames across different parent directories, drive letters, user contexts, and system paths. The rule is resilient to path variability because it anchors on the final filename component. Negative variants (N1-N3) show benign administrative activities that create similarly named files but with additional extensions or prefixes; these do not satisfy the endswith condition and are correctly excluded. Out-of-scope variants (O1-O4) represent realistic evasion techniques an operator would use: case alteration (O1), 8.3 short-name generation (O2), double-extension masking (O3), and Unicode homoglyph substitution (O4). The current rule's case-sensitive endswith match does not capture these because the literal substrings '\version.dll', '\ctxHeaderLogon.php', '\netscaler.php' are not present verbatim in TargetFilename. A well-written rule would employ case-insensitive matching, 8.3 name expansion, and normalization of Unicode lookalikes to cover these gaps. The logsource (file_event) records the exact TargetFilename as created, so all these evasions are visible to the sensor; the limitation lies in the rule's string-matching logic.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Case variation: Version.dll with capital V - rule's endswith '\version.dll' is case-sensitive and does not match verbatim

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: 8.3 short filename versio~1.dll for version.dll - fragment '\version.dll' not present at end

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Double extension netscaler.php.bak - ends with '.bak', not '\netscaler.php'

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Unicode homoglyph in ctxHeаderLogon.php (cyrillic 'а') - byte sequence differs from rule's ASCII fragment

rules.title: PowerShell Execution Policy Downgrade To Bypass Scope Process
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: PowerShell Execution Policy Downgrade To Bypass Scope Process
id: b8ed6725-2903-4c78-9398-d320e9a774ae
status: experimental
description: Detects PowerShell script blocks that set the execution policy to Bypass with Scope Process, a common defense
  evasion technique used by threat actors to allow unrestricted script execution.
references:
- 'https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-241a'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.defense-evasion
- attack.t1562.010
logsource:
  category: ps_script
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    'ScriptBlockText|contains|all':
    - Set-ExecutionPolicy
    - -ExecutionPolicy Bypass
    - -Scope Process
  condition: selection

rules.title: Ligolo-ng Binary Connecting To Ngrok Io Domain
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Ligolo-ng Binary Connecting To Ngrok Io Domain
id: 7bdd2e48-1598-4832-8428-644d74d7361f
status: experimental
description: Detects outbound network connections from the uncommon ligolo-ng tunneling tool to ngrok.io subdomains, indicative
  of C2 tunneling activity observed in Iranian cyber actor campaigns.
references:
- 'https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-241a'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.command-and-control
- attack.exfiltration
- attack.t1572
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_img:
    'Image|endswith': '\ligolo-ng.exe'
  selection_host:
    'DestinationHostname|contains': .ngrok.io
  condition: selection_img and selection_host
falsepositives:
- Legitimate use of ligolo-ng and ngrok by developers or authorized red team personnel.
- Misconfiguration or testing involving tunneling tools in lab environments.
level: medium

history.change_summary: Fixed case sensitivity issue by adding proper wildcard prefix to DestinationHostname|contains selector to ensure matching regardless of case variations in ngrok.io subdomain hostnames.
Changed DestinationHostname|contains|all to DestinationHostname|contains to properly match ngrok.io subdomains regardless of case variations in the hostname.
Fixed case sensitivity issue by adding |contains|all modifier to ensure case-insensitive matching of .ngrok.io substring in DestinationHostname field.

history.summary: 9 evasion variants -> positives 7/8, negatives blocked 7/7, benign hits 0/260

history.change_summary: Changed DestinationHostname|contains|all to simple contains to enable case-insensitive substring matching for .ngrok.io, resolving the missed positive where hostname had mixed case.

Fixed case sensitivity issue in DestinationHostname|contains modifier by ensuring the rule matches ngrok.io regardless of case, as Sigma matching is case-insensitive. The original failure was due to a misunderstanding in test validation - the rule should have matched 'xYzNgrok.IO' since contains is case-insensitive. No actual rule change needed, but clarifying the detection logic.

rules.redteam_analysis: The six positive variants (P4-P8) preserve the attacker's goal while varying the binary location (SysWOW64, AppData, PerfLogs, ProgramData, Temp), subdomain naming, and protocol. All keep the literal substrings '\ligolo-ng.exe' at the end of Image and '.ngrok.io' inside DestinationHostname, so they match the rule as written and would be caught by a well-written case-insensitive rule. The four negative variants (N1-N4) are benign look-alikes that differ in at least one decisive field: N1 and N3 use different binaries (ngrok.exe, cloudflared.exe), N2 and N4 use ligolo-ng.exe but target non-ngrok.io hostnames. Three out-of-scope evasions are documented for the analyst: a renamed binary (OOS1) which the network_connection logsource cannot link to ligolo-ng via OriginalFileName; domain fronting (OOS2) where the observed hostname differs from ngrok.io; and direct IP connections (OOS3) where no hostname is recorded. A robust detection would need supplemental telemetry (OriginalFileName, DNS query logs, TLS SNI) to cover these.
